column1: # Game profile of Monster Train 2 (Switch, update 1.1.1 = v131072). Plays on the Mac and on the iPhone
# Unity 2022.3.54f1 (IL2CPP) with FMOD, SDK 18.3.5 (its sdk is Super Mario Galaxy's build); subsdk0 is the movie module, which plays the intro, an MP4 of H.264 and AAC.
# The shaders are Unity's Shader objects and the post-processing stack's ComputeShader objects in the player's serialized files, which carry no type trees; no bundle lends one, so
# unityfs.py has Unity 2022.3's layouts written out (KNOWN_TREES)
# Controller only (the game reads no touch, docked or handheld): it stays docked (1920x1080) with the 3D pad layout, whose right stick scrolls the route map as the game's prompt shows

# Game name: only a label for profile listings and the Mac window title; the iOS app name is the game name in the base NSP, and the bundle ID comes from the base game title ID (build_ipa.sh / NSP script)
# load order as on Horizon: main, subsdk*, sdk (subsdk0 = NintendoSDK_movie)
# The NPDM declares 16 MB of system resource, so IsVirtualAddressMemoryEnabled is true: nninitStartup hands application pool − used memory to StandardAllocator as virtual address memory
# and never calls SetMemoryHeapSize. The node area cut for this sdk build (dm/tools/sdk_patches.py, Super Mario Galaxy's) shrinks the AddressRegionManager's node area to 62 MB. With the hardware pool
# (3.2 GB) StandardAllocator's region took the alias region to +3.9 GB in nninitStartup; the layout of Ace Attorney Investigations Collection: a 1 GB pool and the 5 GB block
# (256 MB in front + 4.375 GB alias region + 256 MB stack region + 128 MB heap region). Measured on the Mac: the alias region mapped up to +3.25 GB within 90 s and flat for 12 minutes
# (+3.5 GB in a run to the first shop), at most 1.75 GB mapped (the host does not hold the game to the pool, as for Ace Attorney)
# 60 fps (30 on the Switch): the game asks for present interval 2, which display mode ignores, and nothing else in Unity holds it at 30 (about 60 fps on the Mac, the GPU at about
# 2 ms a frame in battle and on the map). Its animations follow the time that really passed (Unity's deltaTime; the PC versions run at any refresh rate): from the same save, screenshots
# at the same moments of the move to the merchant (its fade-in, the greeting) match at 30 and 60 fps (mean difference 3.9), while frame counting would have put 60 fps twice as far
# (11.0, up to 89 in the fade). DM_PRESENT_INTERVAL=game (Documents/env.txt on the iPhone) keeps 30 and saves power
# ---- Shader split (shader_split.py; Unity Shader and ComputeShader objects, read by unityfs.py) ----
# everything is under Data/: the player's serialized files (the post-processing compute shaders in sharedassets2.assets) and the StreamingAssets bundles
